rv.q: Sarah Gordon’s hilarious but ultimately moving comedy about the Brontes is a racy retelling of the sisters’ struggle to become recognised authors.
It’s mightily entertaining if, in the end, limited by its style.
That funniness doesn’t always work to its advantage.
It is quick-witted and amusing though it never deepens enough for the emotional punches to land.
Yet where in this mechanical modernisation is the imaginative power that makes the sisters worth attending to? These Brontës are not other enough.
This play makes her no easier to read.
But the show relies on argument rather than character and it’s short on substance, partly because so little is known about the Brontes beyond their published works.
Gordon commendably crams a lot of information into one eminently (albeit swearily) accessible evening, but it could be said that her potted history falls into that trap, too.
But as an exploration of women who left us such sinewy, sexy, courageous writing, it feels like a sadly wasted opportunity.
That’s when this blistering production hits the wuthering heights.
However, she uses the story as a vehicle for expressing many intriguing ideas and, seen in a production that is acted with conviction and impressively staged, her play is richly entertaining.
It is not the full story, but deceptively satisfying.
Underdog The Other, Other Brontë is an ambitious retelling of history, one which celebrates female strength above all else.
Ultimately Underdog: The Other Other Brontë is different and in a good way.
Weighty topics crop up - the struggles of women, alcoholism, poverty, death from tuberculosis - but there is scarcely time for nuance.
This tedious act of defamation belongs in the bin.
Intelligent and sharply written, Sarah Gordon’s Underdogis, like its take on Charlotte Brontë, imperfect, proud, and utterly captivating.
Arresting performances from Whelan as the deeply unsympathetic Charlotte, Clements as the independent-but-withdrawn Anne and James as the stoical Emily keep Gordon’s spirited play alight.

This version, by Sarah Gordon, directed by Natalie Ibu of Northern Stage, has a more serious purpose. But it executes it with plenty of jokes, a lot of thoroughly modern 'dickhead-and-fuckwit' language, and on a neat outer revolve a lot of quickfire visual jokes and sound effects.

cn.t: A raucous, modernized take on the Brontë sisters' rivalry earns praise for its energy and humor, though critics split on whether Gordon's irreverent approach offers fresh insight or sacrifices depth for superficiality.
